props.title: The Rats
props.initialSlug: Killer rats terrorize New York's subway system

sections.content: **The Rats** (2002) belongs to the often-overlooked made-for-TV creature feature wave of the early 2000s. Following the success of **Locusts** (2005) and **Mansquito** (2005), these films embraced B-movie sensibilities with limited budgets. Starring Madchen Amick of **Twin Peaks** fame, The Rats taps into urban paranoia about vermin infestations while delivering schlocky thrills. It shares DNA with earlier rat horror classics like Willard (1971) and its 2003 remake starring Crispin Glover, though with notably less psychological complexity.

sections.content: The killer rat subgenre has a fascinating history in horror cinema. **Deadly Eyes** (1982) infamously dressed dachshunds in rat costumes when mechanical effects proved insufficient. **Of Unknown Origin** (1983) took a more serious approach, with Peter Weller battling a single intelligent rat in his upscale brownstone. These films reflect evolving urban anxieties, from post-WWII atomic fears to modern concerns about genetic engineering and toxic waste.

The production of **The Rats** (2002) exemplifies early 2000s CGI limitations in TV horror. While theatrical releases like **Pitch Black** (2000) pushed effects boundaries, cable features relied heavily on shadow and suggestion. Director John Lafia, who co-wrote **Child's Play** (1988), brings his horror expertise but struggles with budget constraints. The film's strongest moments focus on claustrophobic tension rather than explicit rat attacks. SUBHEAD: Urban Horror Evolution

sections.content: Modern rat horror has evolved beyond simple creature features. Mulberry Street (2006) uses rat-human hybrids as metaphors for gentrification and urban decay. The documentary **Rats** (2016) proves reality can be more terrifying than fiction, while James Herbert's RAT novel adaptations continue influencing the genre. **The Rats** (2002) marks a transition point between practical effects-driven classics and contemporary CGI-heavy productions.
